'''''Avatar: The Last Airbender''''' (often abbreviated as '''''ATLA''''' and also known as '''''Avatar: The Legend of Aang''''' or simply '''''Avatar'''''<ref>{{Cite web |last=published |first=Alexandra Ramos |date=2025-02-23 |title=I'm Excited For The New Avatar: The Last Airbender Series, But There's One Major Thing I'm Worried About |url=https://www.cinemablend.com/television/im-excited-new-avatar-the-last-airbender-series-one-major-thing-worried-about |access-date=2026-04-28 |website=Cinemablend |language=en}}</ref>) is an American [[animated series|animated]] [[fantasy television|fantasy]] [[Action television|action]] television series created by [[Michael Dante DiMartino]] and [[Bryan Konietzko]]. Produced by [[Nickelodeon Animation Studios]], it originally aired on [[Nickelodeon]] for three seasons from February 2005 to July 2008.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Perlmutter |first1=David |title=The Encyclopedia of American Animated Television Shows |date=2018 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1538103739 |pages=50–51}}</ref>

The series is set in a largely Asian-inspired world in which some people can [[Telekinesis|telekinetically]] manipulate one of the [[Classical element|four elements]]—water, earth, fire or air—through practices known as "bending", inspired by [[Chinese martial arts]]. The only individual who can bend all four elements, the "Avatar", is responsible for maintaining harmony among the world's four nations, and serves as the link between the physical  and spirit worlds. The series follows the journey of twelve-year-old [[Aang]], the current Avatar and last survivor of his nation, the Air Nomads, along with his friends [[Katara (Avatar: The Last Airbender)|Katara]], [[Sokka]], and [[Toph Beifong|Toph]], as they strive to end the Fire Nation's war against the other nations and defeat Fire Lord [[Ozai (Avatar: The Last Airbender)|Ozai]] before he conquers the world. The series also follows [[Zuko]]—the exiled prince of the Fire Nation, seeking to restore his lost honor by capturing Aang, accompanied by his uncle [[Iroh]]—and later, his sister [[Azula]]. ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' is presented and animated in a style that combines Japanese [[anime]] influences with those of [[Modern animation in the United States|American cartoons]] and relies on the imagery of primarily [[Chinese culture]],<ref name=":15">Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko. Avatar: The Last Airbender I.P. Bible.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-02 |title=The Gallery - Elsa Garagarza |url=https://www.animenewsnetwork.com/the-gallery/2009-01-31 |access-date=2024-10-02 |website=Anime News Network |language=en}}</ref> with various other influences from different [[East Asia]]n, [[Southeast Asia]]n, [[South Asia]]n, [[North Asia]]n, and [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|indigenous American]] cultures.

''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' was a ratings success and received widespread acclaim from critics and audiences, with high praise given to its characters, cultural references, art direction, voice acting, soundtrack, humor, ending, and thematic content. The series explores themes rarely touched on in youth entertainment, such as [[war]], [[genocide]], [[sexism]], [[gender role]]s, [[imperialism]], [[totalitarianism]], [[class conflict|class warfare]], [[political corruption]], [[indoctrination]], [[cruelty to animals|animal cruelty]], [[destiny|fate]], and [[Freedom of choice|free choice]].<ref name="Vice"/> It won five [[Annie Awards]], a [[Genesis Awards|Genesis Award]], a [[Primetime Emmy Award]], a [[Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards|Kids' Choice Award]], and a [[Peabody Award]]. Since its release, the show has been regarded by critics as one of the most acclaimed series of the 21st century, and one of the greatest animated television series of all time.<!-- Sources are listed in the Legacy section of this article; please DO NOT remove without talk page consensus --> It is also considered Nickelodeon's [[magnum opus|''magnum opus'']].

novel series]], two animated sequel series, a [[The Last Airbender (film)|live-action film]], and a [[Netflix]] [[Avatar: The Last Airbender (2024 TV series)|live-action adaptation series]].<ref == Series overview ==
=== Setting ===
{{Redirect|Fire Nation|the Native American tribe|Mascouten}}{{See also|World of Avatar: The Last Airbender{{!}}World of ''Avatar: The Last Airbender''}}[[File:Avatar world map.jpg|thumb|left|alt=world map|A map of the four nations]]
''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' is set in a world where human civilization consists of four nations, named after the four [[classical element]]s: the Water Tribe, the Earth Kingdom, the Fire Nation, and the Air Nomads. In each nation, certain people, known as "benders" (waterbenders, earthbenders, firebenders, and airbenders), have the ability to [[Telekinesis|telekinetically]] manipulate and control the element corresponding to their nation, using gestures based on [[Chinese martial arts]]. The "Avatar" is the only individual with the ability to bend all four elements.

The Avatar is an international arbiter whose duty is to maintain harmony among the four nations, and act as a mediator between humans and spirits. When the Avatar dies, their spirit is [[Reincarnation|reincarnated]] in a new body, who will be born to parents in the next nation in a set order known as the Avatar cycle: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth. By tradition, the new Avatar will travel the world to learn all four bending arts, after which they will begin in earnest their role as global peacekeeper. The Avatar can enter a condition known as the "Avatar State", in which they temporarily gain the skills and knowledge of all their past incarnations. Although this is when they are at their most powerful, if the Avatar were ever killed while in the Avatar State, the reincarnation cycle would be broken and the Avatar would cease to exist.

=== <span class="anchor" id="Book One: Water"></span><span class="anchor" id="Book Two: Earth"></span><span class="anchor" id="Book Three: Fire"></span>Synopsis ===
A century ago, young Avatar [[Aang]], afraid of his new responsibilities, fled from his home and was forced into the ocean by a storm. He encased himself and his sky bison Appa in [[suspended animation]] in an iceberg near the South Pole. Shortly afterward, Fire Lord Sozin, the ruler of the Fire Nation, launched a [[world war]] to expand his nation's empire. Knowing that the Avatar must be an Air Nomad, he and his army carried out a [[genocide]] against the Air Nomads, which he timed with the arrival of a [[comet]] that gives firebenders tremendous power. A hundred years later, siblings [[Katara (Avatar: The Last Airbender)|Katara]] and [[Sokka]], teenagers of the Southern Water Tribe, accidentally discover Aang and revive him.

In the first season, Aang travels with Katara and Sokka to the Northern Water Tribe to learn waterbending and be prepared to defeat the Fire Nation. Prince [[Zuko]], the banished son of Fire Lord Ozai, pursues them, accompanied by his uncle [[Iroh]], hoping to capture the Avatar in order to restore his honor. Aang is also pursued by Zhao, a Fire Nation admiral aspiring to win Ozai's favor. When his navy attacks the Northern Water Tribe, Zhao kills the moon spirit; Yue, the princess of the tribe, sacrifices her life to revive it, and Aang drives off the enemy fleet.

In the second season, Aang learns earthbending from [[Toph Beifong]], a blind earthbending prodigy. Zuko and Iroh become refugees in the Earth Kingdom, eventually settling in its capital Ba Sing Se. Aang's group travels to Ba Sing Se to seek the Earth King's support for an attack on the Fire Nation during an upcoming [[solar eclipse]], during which firebenders will be powerless. Both groups are pursued by [[Azula]], Zuko's younger sister. Azula infiltrates Ba Sing Se and instigates a [[coup d'état]] against the Earth King, bringing the capital under Fire Nation control. Zuko betrays Iroh and returns to the Fire Nation.

In the third season, Aang and his allies invade the Fire Nation during the eclipse, but are forced to retreat. Zuko abandons the Fire Nation to teach Aang firebending. Aang, raised to respect all life, wrestles with the possibility that he will have to kill Ozai to end the war. When Sozin's comet returns, Aang confronts Ozai and uses his Avatar powers to strip Ozai of his firebending ability; meanwhile, Aang's friends liberate Ba Sing Se, destroy the Fire Nation airship fleet, and capture Azula. Zuko is crowned the new Fire Lord and the war comes to an end.

=== Episodes ===

{{See also|Sozin's Comet}}
The series consists of sixty-one episodes. The first episode—an-hour-long premiere—aired on February 21, 2005, on [[Nickelodeon]].<ref name="Iceberg">{{cite web |url=http://tv.ign.com/objects/142/14228011.html |title=The Boy in the Iceberg |access-date=July 21, 2008 |website=Avatar: The Last Airbender |publisher=IGN |date=February 21, 2005 |archive-date=April 25, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425072322/http://tv.ign.com/objects/142/14228011.html |url-status=live}}</ref> The series concluded with a two-hour television movie broadcast on July 19, 2008.<ref name="TV Guide">{{cite web |url=https://www.tvguide.com/tvshows/avatar-the-last-airbender/episodes/194673/ |title=Sozin's Comet |access-date=July 21, 2008 |website=Avatar: The Last Airbender |publisher=[[TV Guide]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130825082159/http://www.tvguide.com/detail/tv-show.aspx?tvobjectid=194673&more=ucepisodelist&episodeid=8082181 |archive-date=August 25, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> Each season of the series is known as a "book", in which each episode is referred to as a "chapter". Each book takes its name from one of the elements Aang must master: Water, Earth, and Fire.<ref name="Iceberg" /> The show's first two seasons each consists of twenty episodes and the third season twenty-one. The entire series has been released on [[DVD]] in [[DVD region code|regions]] 1, 2, and 4.<ref name="TVShowsOnDVD Release Dates">{{cite web |url=http://www.tvshowsondvd.com/shows/Avatar-Airbender/8931 |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender on DVD |access-date=October 28, 2008 |date=February 24, 2005 |publisher=[[TVShowsOnDVD.com]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081017180706/http://www.tvshowsondvd.com/shows/Avatar-Airbender/8931 |archive-date=October 17, 2008 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

{{As of|2020|05|post=,}} the complete series is available on [[Netflix]] in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender |url=https://www.netflix.com/nz/title/70142405 |publisher=[[Netflix]] |access-date=December 25, 2019 |archive-date=January 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200129000922/https://www.netflix.com/nz/title/70142405 |url-status=live}}</ref> It became the most popular show on U.S. Netflix within the first week of its release there, despite not being featured on the main page.<ref name=":14" /> The show broke the record for longest consecutive appearance on Netflix's daily top ten list, with 60 straight days on the list, one of only two shows in the top ten record holders that was not a Netflix original series as of July 2020.<ref name="Newsweek" /> Later in June 2020, the complete series became available on [[Paramount+]] (at the time CBS All Access)<ref name="Paramount+" /> and later on [[Amazon Prime Video]]<ref name="Prime" /> in January 2021.

== Development ==
=== Conception and production ===
{{multiple image
| align             = right
| total_width       = 300
| image1            = MichaelDanteDiMartinoCCJuly09.jpg
| width1            = 533
| height1           = 800
| alt1              = Bald man with glasses smiling
| image2            = BryanKonietzkoCCJuly09.jpg

The creators and producers of ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'', [[Michael Dante DiMartino]] and [[Bryan Konietzko]], met at a Halloween party in 1995 during their time as students in the [[Rhode Island School of Design]], and began their professional partnership later that year when Konietzko assisted DiMartino in painting backgrounds and cels for the latter's student film. DiMartino and Konietzko moved to Los Angeles in 1996 and 1998 respectively to pursue careers in the animation industry. In between jobs, DiMartino animated a short titled ''Atomic Love'' that he pitched as a TV series, but was unsuccessful due to the amount of robot-based animated series already in development. During Konietzko's stint as an art director on ''[[Invader Zim]]'', he and DiMartino formulated the idea of pitching a coming-to-age series based on their childhoods, but were too busy with their respective jobs to solidify the concept. When ''Invader Zim'' was abruptly canceled in January 2002, Konietzko declared to DiMartino his resolution to get their idea made at all cost.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=10}}

By this time, Konietzko had established a good relationship with [[Nickelodeon]] head of development [[Eric Coleman (producer)|Eric Coleman]], who was interested in the prospect of Konietzko creating and pitching his own show. Upon the end of his job on ''Invader Zim'', Konietzko met with Coleman, introduced him to DiMartino and discussed their intent to create a series that held heart and integrity while meeting the network's commercial requirements. Although their meeting went well, Coleman revealed that the network was not looking for coming-of-age stories based on human characters. He added that the network was following the success of the ''[[The Lord of the Rings (film series)|Lord of the Rings]]'' and ''[[Harry Potter (film series)|Harry Potter]]'' film series and was thus searching for non-violent action and adventure concepts with an emphasis on legends and lore. Lastly, he established that the show would require the point-of-view of either a kid hero or a non-human character, emphasizing that middle-aged human protagonists would be off-brand for Nickelodeon. Konietzko concluded the meeting with the promise of a pitch along those directives within a month.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=10}}

DiMartino and Konietzko indiscriminately laid out their conceptual sketches in their effort to establish a new idea. Among them was a sketch that Konietzko created during his time on ''Invader Zim'', which featured a robot cyclops monkey with an arrow on his head and holding a staff, a balding middle-aged man in a futuristic outfit, and a bipedal polar bear-dog hybrid. Konietzko's sketch, a "half-baked" sci-fi adventure, was primarily influenced by ''[[Cowboy Bebop]]''. Recalling Coleman's advice against middle-aged main characters, Konietzko redrew the human character as a boy, but retained his baldness and transferred the robot's staff and arrow to him. After adding the new drawing to the collection of sketches, Konietzko began drawing other fanciful animal hybrids, which culminated in a drawing of a good-natured and nomadic "[[Huckleberry Finn|Huck Finnesque]]" boy herding a group of flying bison-manatee hybrids. The sketch was influenced by the works of renowned [[anime]] film director [[Hayao Miyazaki]], of whom Konietzko and DiMartino were fans.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|pp=10–11}}

DiMartino drew inspiration for what would become the Southern Water Tribe from a documentary on the [[Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition]], and he pitched Konietzko the idea of a group of people similarly trapped in the South Pole.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=12}} Two weeks after their meeting with Coleman, Konietzko was suddenly inspired by DiMartino's idea and formulated a concept of a group of children in the South Pole who were terrorized by "fire people" and rescued by the young nomad from his earlier drawing.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=12}}<ref name="NickMagInterview1">{{cite journal |last=DiMartino |first=Michael Dante |author2=Konietzko, Bryan |year=2006 |title=In Their Elements |journal=Nickelodeon Magazine |issue=Winter 2006 |page=6}}</ref> Konietzko and DiMartino reconvened that evening and began developing the series' setting over the next two weeks.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=12}} Although DiMartino and Konietzko were themselves fans of the two successful British fantasy series that Nickelodeon sought to emulate, the pair chose to differentiate their own series by inserting influences from Asian cultures and philosophies, traditional [[martial arts]], [[yoga]], anime, and [[Cinema of Hong Kong|Hong Kong cinema]].{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=12}}<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2007/09/06/interview-avatars-bryan-konietzko-and-michael-dante-dimartino |title=Interview: Avatar's Bryan Konietzko and Michael Dante DiMartino |date=September 6, 2007 |website=IGN |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071118151020/http://tv.ign.com/articles/818/818284p1.html |archive-date=November 18, 2007}}</ref> The co-creators successfully pitched the concept to Coleman with early sketches of [[Aang]], [[Katara (Avatar: The Last Airbender)|Katara]], and [[Sokka]], three color images depicting the desired action, adventure, and magic aspects, and a description of the series' characters, setting and full story arc.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=12}}<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.awn.com/animationworld/its-elementary-avatar-last-airbender |title=It's Elementary&nbsp;– Avatar: The Last Airbender |last=Clark |first=Craig J. |date=October 17, 2007 |publisher=Animation World Magazine, Inc. |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080120150858/http://www.worldscreen.com/newscurrent.php?filename=bit022607.htm |archive-date=January 20, 2008}}</ref> The series was introduced to the public in a teaser reel at [[San Diego Comic-Con International|Comic-Con]] in July 2004,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Baisley |first1=Sarah |title=Comic-Con International 2004 Report |url=http://www.awn.com/animationworld/comic-con-international-2004-report |publisher=[[Animation World Network]] |date=September 9, 2004 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303221846/http://www.awn.com/animationworld/comic-con-international-2004-report |archive-date=March 3, 2016}}</ref> and premiered on February 21, 2005.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.awn.com/news/nick-premieres-avatar-hour-special-feb-21 |title=Nick Premieres Avatar in Hour Special Feb. 21 |last=Baisley |first=Sarah |date=February 18, 2005 |publisher=[[Animation World Network]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171027031527/https://www.awn.com/news/nick-premieres-avatar-hour-special-feb-21 |archive-date=October 27, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

According to head writer [[Aaron Ehasz]], Konietzko and DiMartino originally envisioned the series as three seasons long. However, Nickelodeon asked Ehasz about his ideas for a potential fourth season, which he later discussed with both Konietzko and DiMartino. Ehasz believed that a fourth season would be created, but this plan was interrupted when Konietzko and DiMartino decided to focus on assisting [[M. Night Shyamalan]] as executive producers for ''[[The Last Airbender (film)|The Last Airbender]]'' film. Ehasz claims that Shyamalan insisted they create a fourth season, but Konietzko and DiMartino wanted to work on the live-action film and reverted to the original three-season plan.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-04-03 |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender's Writer Says a Possible Season 4 Was Sidelined for Shyamalan's Film |url=https://gizmodo.com/avatar-the-last-airbenders-writer-says-a-possible-seas-1833776084 |access-date=2022-10-18 |website=Gizmodo |language=en |archive-date=October 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221019001122/https://gizmodo.com/avatar-the-last-airbenders-writer-says-a-possible-seas-1833776084 |url-status=live}}</ref> Konietzko and DiMartino have denied Ehasz's statements, asserting that a fourth season was never considered by them or Nickelodeon.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Patches |first=Matt |date=2020-08-31 |title=Legend of Korra creators look back at the prescient series |url=https://www.polygon.com/animation-cartoons/2020/8/31/21405084/legend-of-korra-netflix-bryan-konietzko-michael-dimartino-interview-avatar |access-date=2022-10-19 |website=Polygon |language=en-US}}</ref> Shyamalan has made comments that align with Ehasz's, such as acknowledging uncertainty at the time about whether the series would conclude after three seasons. Supporting the animated series going beyond three seasons, he nevertheless refused to sign on for the live-action adaptation, as he wanted to direct a trilogy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=LAF {{!}} Last Airbender Fans {{!}} Legend of Korra News {{!}} Home |url=https://www.lastairbenderfans.com/index.php?start_from=&ucat=8&subaction=showfull&id=1269959997&archive=1272555212& |access-date=2025-02-17 |website=www.lastairbenderfans.com}}</ref>

=== Pilot ===
A [[pilot episode]] for the series was made in 2003. It was animated by Tin House, Inc., written by DiMartino and Konietzko, and directed by [[Dave Filoni]]. [[Mitchel Musso]] voiced Aang in this pilot but was later replaced by [[Zach Tyler Eisen]] when the show began production. In the episode, Sokka and his sister Kya (renamed Katara by the time the series aired) must travel the world to find masters for Aang, who is the Avatar; however, they must evade a critical foe, Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation, who wants to capture Aang.

This episode was first publicly released as one of the extras in the [[NTSC]] season 1 [[DVD]] [[box set]], which were not available with the previously released individual volumes. As the [[PAL]] box set lacks extras, the episode was not made available on DVD in PAL regions. The episode was released with audio commentary from the creators which, unlike commentary on other episodes in the season, is not possible to disable on the DVD set.<ref name="dvd talk">{{cite web |url=https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/24067/avatar-the-last-airbender-the-complete-book-1-collection/ |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender&nbsp;— The Complete Book 1 Collection |last=Rich |first=Jamie S. |date=September 27, 2006 |publisher=DVDTalk.com |access-date=May 4, 2008 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090507145932/http://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/24067/avatar-the-last-airbender-the-complete-book-1-collection/ |archive-date=May 7, 2009}}</ref> On June 14, 2010, the unaired pilot was made available with and without commentary for the first time via the [[iTunes Store]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://itunes.apple.com/us/tv-season/avatar-last-airbender-season/id373383858 |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender, Season 1: Essentials Collection on iTunes |website=iTunes |access-date=May 4, 2018 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210015757/http://itunes.apple.com/us/tv-season/avatar-last-airbender-season/id373383858 |archive-date=February 10, 2012}}</ref> In 2020, the pilot was streamed on [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Nickelodeon Streams Unaired Avatar: The Last Airbender Pilot |url=https://screenrant.com/avatar-last-airbender-unaired-pilot-episode-video-nickelodeon/ |website=ScreenRant |access-date=August 15, 2020 |date=August 15, 2020 |url-status=live |archive-date=August 15, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200815061256/https://screenrant.com/avatar-last-airbender-unaired-pilot-episode-video-nickelodeon/}}</ref>

=== Influences ===
[[File:The Forbidden City - View from Coal Hill.jpg|thumb|upright=1.31|Fictional locations featured in the show are based on the architecture and designs of real locations. For example, the creators modeled the city of Ba Sing Se off the [[Forbidden City]] in [[Beijing]], China.]]
The series is notable for its extensive influence from [[East Asia|East Asian]] [[Culture of East Asia|culture]], [[History of Eastern art|art]] and [[East Asian mythology|mythology]] for its universe, especially [[Chinese culture]].<ref name=":15" /> Its creators employed cultural consultant Edwin Zane and [[Chinese calligraphy|Chinese calligrapher]] Siu-Leung Lee to help determine its art direction and settings.<ref name="nytimes" /><ref>{{cite news |url=https://movies.nytimes.com/person/537590/Edwin-Zane/filmography |title=Edwin Zane&nbsp;— Filmography |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090221075453/http://movies.nytimes.com/person/537590/Edwin-Zane/filmography |archive-date=February 21, 2009 |department=Movies & TV Dept. |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The creators have cited [[Chinese art]] and [[History of China|history]], [[Hinduism]], [[Taoism]] and [[Buddhism]], and [[yoga]] as the strongest influences on the series.<ref name="nytimes">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/08/28/arts/television/28lass.html |title=Kung Fu Fightin' Anime Stars, Bo |author=Mark Lasswell |date=August 25, 2005 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080327052334/http://shop.nickjr.com/category/index.jsp?categoryId=2426272&cp=2060004 |archive-date=March 27, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nicksplat.com/Whatsup/200510/12000135.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071217111256/http://www.nicksplat.com/Whatsup/200510/12000135.html |archive-date=December 17, 2007 |title=Interview With The Creators |date=October 12, 2005 |publisher=NickSplat.com}}</ref>

[[Jeremy Zuckerman]] and [[Benjamin Wynn]] created the series' music and sound design together in the early developmental stages and then went on to divide the tasks, with Zuckerman taking on the musical composition and Wynn the sound design. They experimented with a wide range of instruments, including the [[guzheng]], [[pipa]], and [[duduk]], to match the show's Asian-influenced setting.<ref name="Brennan 2008">{{cite web |url=https://www.soundtrack.net/content/article/?id=252 |last=Brennan |first=Mike |date=2008-04-07 |title=An interview with Jeremy Zuckerman and Benjamin Wynn |access-date=August 20, 2009 |publisher=[[Soundtrack.Net]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121103200700/http://www.soundtrack.net/content/article/?id=252 |archive-date=November 3, 2012 }}</ref>

The art style of the fictitious locations featured in the series are based on real locations in Asia. Sites such as the [[Forbidden City]] and the [[Great Wall of China]] in [[Beijing]] were inspirations for the Earth Kingdom city of Ba Sing Se,{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|pp=130–172}} and Water Tribe locations were based on [[Inuit]] and [[Sirenik Eskimos|Sireniki]] cultures.<ref name="Vice" /> According to Ehasz, early Fire Nation designs were based on Japanese culture. To avoid accidentally making broad statements, they redesigned many settings and peoples to be more "broadly inspired".<ref name="Vice" /> For the final design, the creators went with a more Chinese style for the Fire Nation's clothing and architecture.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=25}} For instance, the Fire Temple was based on the [[Yellow Crane Tower]], as its flame-like architectural elements were considered a perfect motif for the Fire Nation architecture, according to the creators.{{sfn|Konietzko|DiMartino|2010|p=52}}

The gestures used by the "bender" characters are derived from [[Chinese martial arts]], for which the creators employed Sifu Kisu of the Harmonious Fist Chinese Athletic Association as a consultant.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.harmoniousfist.com/ |title=The National Shaolin Information Resource |publisher=The Harmonious Fist Chinese Athletic Association |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061205044333/http://harmoniousfist.com/ |archive-date=December 5, 2006 |url-status=dead |access-date=January 10, 2006}}</ref> Each fighting style is unique to the "benders" who use them or characters who are aligned to a certain element. For example, practitioners of "waterbending" use movements influenced by [[tai chi]] and focus on alignment, body structure, breath, and visualization. [[Hung Ga]]r was the inspiration for practitioners of "earthbending", and was chosen for its firmly rooted stances and powerful strikes as a representation of the solidity of earth. [[Northern Shaolin]], which uses strong arm and leg movements, was chosen to represent "firebending". ''[[Baguazhang]]'', which uses dynamic circular movements and quick directional changes, was used for "airbending".<ref>{{cite AV media |people=Sifu Kisu |title=Creating the Legend |publisher=Nickelodeon}}</ref> The Chu Gar [[Southern Praying Mantis]] style can be seen practiced by the earthbender, [[Toph]], who develops a unique fighting style as a result of her blindness.<ref name="con">{{cite web |url=http://flaming-june.org/videos/Audience%20Question%20&%20Answer%20Pt.%202.wmv |title=Audience Questions and Answer Part 2 at the San Diego Comi-con 2006 |publisher=Flaming June |access-date=May 7, 2008 |format=WMV |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080414152845/http://flaming-june.org/videos/Audience%20Question%20%26%20Answer%20Pt.%202.wmv |archive-date=April 14, 2008 |url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Cinema of Asia|Asian cinema]] also influenced the presentation of these martial-art bending moves.<ref name="NickMagInterview1"/>

== Themes ==
The series addresses many topics rarely touched on in youth entertainment, including issues relating to war, [[genocide]], [[imperialism]], [[colonialism]] and [[totalitarianism]], [[Sexism|gender discrimination]] and [[Women's empowerment|female empowerment]], [[Social exclusion|marginalization]] and [[oppression]], and spirituality, as well as philosophical questions surrounding fate, destiny, and free will.<ref name="Vice"/>

The show is set during a period in which the world is engulfed in an imperialistic war initiated by the Fire Nation. While war is a constant backdrop, the show depicts these effects through the eyes of common people{{mdash}}the oppressed Earth Kingdom citizens as well as indoctrinated Fire Nation schoolchildren{{mdash}}to show how war can and does make victims of everyone.<ref name="Vice"/> While the Fire Nation is presented as the instigator of violence, the show also depicts the systemic inequality experienced by residents in the Earth Kingdom city of Ba Sing Se as well as the nefarious activities of the city's  corrupt secret police. These situations show the corrupting nature of power and the nuances of good and evil.<ref name="Vice"/> The show introduces viewers to genocide early on when protagonist Aang visits his former home in the Southern Air Temple. He arrives to discover his people have been massacred and displays a range of emotions, such as rage, guilt, and sadness.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.avclub.com/avatar-the-last-airbender-the-southern-air-temple-1798168504 |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender: "The Southern Air Temple"/"The Warriors Of Kyoshi" |website=[[The A.V. Club]] |author=Childs, Hayden |date=June 7, 2011 |access-date=July 28, 2018 |archive-date=October 8, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181008022722/https://tv.avclub.com/avatar-the-last-airbender-the-southern-air-temple-1798168504 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The character Zuko and his relationship with his father and Uncle Iroh is the main [[Character arc|redemption arc]] of the series, and represents the show's message that destiny is not binding but rather can be changed.<ref name=":0"/> In season two, Zuko struggles to conform to the destiny and path determined by his father,<ref name="Vice"/> but Iroh prods him, asking, "who are you, what do ''you'' want?"<ref name=kirk/>

The show also represents a diverse cast of characters in order to tackle the issue of marginalization. For example, in introducing a blind character like Toph and a [[Paraplegia|paraplegic]] boy like Teo, the show depicts characters with vulnerabilities overcoming their physical and societal limitations.<ref name="Vice"/> This is also true when it comes to the show's female characters. For example, female protagonist Katara faces systemic sexism when she reaches the Northern Water Tribe to learn waterbending, only to learn that girls and women are prohibited from doing so; a rule that is deeply ingrained within the culture. In another example, her brother Sokka initially espouses sexist viewpoints and is dismissive of the all-female Kyoshi Warriors, but learns to respect and appreciate their skills and mature as a person and fighter.<ref name="Vice"/> According to Kirk Hamilton of ''[[Kotaku]]'', these themes represent the show's message that it is more important to be oneself than to hew to societal expectations.<ref name=kirk/>

== Reception ==
=== Ratings ===
''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' was the highest-rated animated television series in its demographic at its premiere; an average of 1.1&nbsp;million viewers watched each new episode.<ref name="animation">{{cite web |url=http://www.animationinsider.net/article.php?articleID=1066 |title=Avatar: Season 3 |date=June 30, 2006 |last=Bynum |first=Aaron H. |publisher=Animation Insider |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070207054907/http://www.animationinsider.net/article.php?articleID=1066 |archive-date=February 7, 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref> and was a highly rated part of the [[Nicktoons]] lineup beyond its 6-to-11-year-old target demographic.<ref name="DemographicandPlot">{{cite web |url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/news/e3ida90dc7b5e3c5134350d27182974c222 |title=Element of Shyamalan in "Airbender" |last=Kit |first=Borys |date=January 9, 2007 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |publisher=Nielsen Business Media, Inc. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070111051521/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/news/e3ida90dc7b5e3c5134350d27182974c222 |archive-date=January 11, 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref> A one-hour special, ''The Secret of the Fire Nation'', consisting of the episodes "The Serpent's Pass" and "The Drill", aired on September 15, 2006, and attracted 4.1&nbsp;million viewers. According to the [[Nielsen ratings]], the special was the fifth highest-rated [[cable television]] program that week.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.animationinsider.net/article.php?articleID=1153 |title=Secret of the Fire Nation Ratings |date=September 20, 2006 |last=Bynum |first=Aaron H. |publisher=Animation Insider |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207201044/http://www.animationinsider.net/article.php?articleID=1153 |archive-date=February 7, 2012}}</ref> In 2007, ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' was syndicated in more than 105&nbsp;countries and was one of Nickelodeon's top-rated programs. The series ranked first on Nickelodeon in Germany, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Colombia.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.viacom.com/NEWS/NewsText.aspx?RID=1077954 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071115025920/http://www.viacom.com/NEWS/NewsText.aspx?RID=1077954 |archive-date=November 15, 2007 |title=Aang Is Ready to Strike Down the Fire Nation on the Darkest Day of the Year in Avatar's "Day of Black Sun" Premiering Friday, Nov. 30 on Nickelodeon | work=News |publisher=Viacom |date=November 14, 2007}}</ref>

The four-part series finale, "[[Sozin's Comet]]", had the highest ratings of the series. Its first airing averaged 5.6 million viewers, 195&nbsp;percent more than Nickelodeon had in mid-July 2007.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Umstead |first=R. Thomas |date=July 28, 2008 |title=Originals Score Big Ratings |url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/A181901036/ITOF?u=wikipedia&sid=bookmark-ITOF&xid=3dc52fae |access-date=April 18, 2026 |magazine=[[Multichannel News]] |publisher=[[Future US]] |page=33 |via=[[Gale (publisher)|Gale]] |volume=29 |issue=29}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |date=December 18–24, 2006 |title=In Brief: Avatar's Big Finish |journal=TV Guide |page=12}}</ref> During the week of July 14, it was the most-viewed program by the under-14 demographic.<ref>{{cite web |last=Diaz |first=Glenn L. |date=July 29, 2008 |title=19 Million Tuned in for Special "Avatar" Week |url=https://www.buddytv.com/19-million-tuned-in-for-special-avatar-week/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221025173541/https://www.buddytv.com/19-million-tuned-in-for-special-avatar-week/ |archive-date=October 25, 2022 |publisher=Buddytv.com |access-date=October 25, 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.animationinsider.net/article.php?articleID=1794 |title=Nick's "AVATAR" Animation Series Finale Scores Big Ratings |publisher=Animationinsider.net |last=Luna |first=Kyle |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090105224926/http://www.animationinsider.net/article.php?articleID=1794 |archive-date=January 5, 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The finale's popularity was reflected in online media; ''Rise of the Phoenix King'', a [[Nick.com]] online game based on "Sozin's Comet", had almost 815,000 plays in three days.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://www.animationmagazine.net/article/8636 |title=Nick's Avatar Hits Ratings High |last=Ball |first=Ryan |magazine=[[Animation Magazine]] |date=July 23, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080728160736/http://www.animationmagazine.net/article/8636 |archive-date=July 28, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Amith praised its sophisticated storylines, edginess, humor, and action.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://j-entonline.com/blu-ray-dvd-reviews/dvd-reviews-film-tv/avatar-the-last-airbender-the-complete-book-1-collectors-edition-a-j-ent-dvd-review/ |title=Avatar: the Last Airbender: The Complete Book 1 – Collector's Edition (a J!-ENT DVD Review) |last=Amith |first=Dennis |date=June 9, 2010 |website=j-entonline.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080915224547/http://www.oafe.net/articulation/0707.php |archive-date=September 15, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> Franco "Cricket" Te of Nerd Society described ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' as "one of the best cartoon[s]" he had ever seen, recommending the series for its characters and plot.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |url=http://www.nerdsociety.com/dvd-review-avatar-the-last-airbender-the-complete-book-1-collectors-edition/ |title=DVD Review: Avatar: The Last Airbender – The Complete Book 1 (Collector's Edition) |last=Te |first=Franco |date=June 22, 2010 |publisher=Nerd Society |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080126052639/http://community.livejournal.com/avatar_fans/1658088.html |archive-date=January 26, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> Scott Thill of ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' called the series engaging and its setting, influenced by the Eastern world, "fantastic".<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.wired.com/2010/06/last-airbender-dvd-box/ |title=Bend Our Minds, Win Avatar: The Last Airbender DVD Box |last=Thill |first=Scott |date=June 22, 2010 |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170928015534/https://www.wired.com/2010/06/last-airbender-dvd-box/ |archive-date=September 28, 2017 |url-status=live |language=en-US}}</ref>
Kirk Hamilton of ''[[Kotaku]]'' said the series should be considered part of the [[Golden Age of Television (2000s–present)|Golden Age of Television]], and recommended "the sophisticated kids show" to others.<ref name="kirk">{{Cite web |url=https://kotaku.com/avatar-the-last-airbender-is-one-of-the-great-tv-shows-1787285748 |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender Is One Of The Greatest TV Shows Of All Time |last=Hamilton |first=Kirk |date=February 28, 2017 |website=Kotaku |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170731200915/https://kotaku.com/avatar-the-last-airbender-is-one-of-the-great-tv-shows-1787285748 |archive-date=July 31, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The show's writing and themes have been widely lauded by critics. Michael S. Mammano of ''Den of Geek'' called the plot "smartly-written" and praised the animation.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.denofgeek.com/us/tv/avatar/248639/avatar-the-last-airbender-the-complete-series-coming |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender – The Complete Series Coming |last=Mammano |first=Michael |date=August 24, 2015 |work=Den of Geek |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070827215413/http://www.pgnx.net/news.php?page=full&id=14399 |archive-date=August 27, 2007 |url-status=dead |language=en}}</ref> Nicole Clark, writing for [[Vice News]], stated that the show's narrative depth was "its greatest asset", and praised the story's "emotional authenticity" and how it "expose[d] very young viewers to darker subject matter, like genocide and authoritarianism, while giving them a framework for understanding these issues."<ref name="Vice">{{cite web |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/avatar-the-last-airbender-is-still-one-of-the-greatest-shows-of-all-time/ |title='Avatar: The Last Airbender' Is Still One of the Greatest Shows of All Time |publisher=[[Vice News]] |author=Clark, Nicole |date=July 20, 2018 |access-date=July 28, 2018 |archive-date=May 14, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210514191333/https://www.vice.com/en/article/5943jz/avatar-the-last-airbender-is-still-one-of-the-greatest-shows-of-all-time |url-status=live}}</ref> Jenifer Rosenberg of ComicMix praised the program's emphasis on family, friends, community, and education.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |url=http://www.comicmix.com/2010/06/20/review-avatar-the-last-airbender-the-complete-book-1-collectors-edition/ |title=Review: 'Avatar: The Last Airbender: The Complete Book 1 Collector's Edition' {{!}} ComicMix |last=Rosenburg |first=Jenifer |date=June 20, 2010 |publisher=ComicMix |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160312162151/http://www.comicmix.com/2010/06/20/review-avatar-the-last-airbender-the-complete-book-1-collectors-edition/ |archive-date=March 12, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> According to Hartel, the series touches on themes of "genocide and self-doubt" without frightening younger children; rogue characters are redeemable, sending an important message that people can change and are not bonded to "destiny".<ref name=":0"/> Chris Mitchell called the plot "fantastic".<ref name=":4"/> D. F. Smith compared the series' plot to Japanese anime, calling its tone and dialogue "very American" and praising the humor leavening an epic, dramatic theme suitable for all ages.<ref name=":5"/> Rob Keyes also praised the series' humor and affecting plot, saying, "[It] will capture your hearts".<ref name=":6"/>

According to Noyes, the series amalgamates elements of "classic fantasy epics".<ref name=":7"/> Douglass Jr. called the plot engaging, well-thought-out, and meaningful, stating that the series' concept was "well-realized", with a consistent story. Douglass wrote that the characters "[have] a real sense of progression", and praised the writers for their humor, drama, and emotion.<ref name=":8"/> Joshua Miller called the series surprisingly dark despite its "silly" theme, saying that the plot is livelier than that of ''[[Lost (2004 TV series)|Lost]]'' and, similar to the latter show, emphasizes character development. According to Miller, its writing was "true adult levels of storytelling".<ref name=":9"/> Janson described the series as more than fantasy- and superhero-themed, seeing the characters as central and relatable.<ref name=":10"/> "Cricket" Te praised the series' use of [[Buddhist philosophy|Buddhist philosophies]] and the diverse presentation of its themes of courage and life.<ref name=":11"/> Hamilton praised the series for encouraging its audience to be themselves and for its quiet progressivism.<ref name=kirk/>

Steven Pearce of ''[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]'' described ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' as a landmark of Western children's animation, praising its intelligent writing, character development, thoughtful and sometimes dark storylines, humor, strong female characters, and incorporation of Asian and Pacific cultural and philosophical influences. He also highlighted the series' treatment of politics and its considerable influence on subsequent animation.<ref name=":04">{{Cite web |last=Pearce|first=Steven|date=2019|title=SFE: Avatar: The Last Airbender|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/avatar_the_last_airbender|access-date=2026-05-11|website=The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction}}</ref>

Critics also praised ''Avatar: The Last Airbender''{{'}}s character development, art, animation, and choreography; Eric Amaya enjoyed the expressive animation that complemented the writing. According to Amaya, elements were influenced by the work of [[Hayao Miyazaki]].<ref name=":1"/> Douglass Jr. called the character development interesting,<ref name=":8"/> while Nicole Clark wrote that the show "managed to do what so few shows even today have: assemble a cast of characters that depicts the world as it is, with a range of identities and experiences."<ref name="Vice"/> Rosenburg praised the series' portrayal of its female characters as "strong, responsible, [and] intelligent".<ref name=":12"/> According to Miller, the bender characters' use of bending for everyday activities brought "depth and believability" to the Avatar world. Miller called the series' designs "rich and immersive", with each nation having its own, detailed look. He praised the action scenes as "well rendered", comparing the development of the ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' world to that of ''[[The Lord of the Rings (film series)|The Lord of the Rings]]'', and the fight choreography as "wonderful in its most minor details".<ref name=":9"/> Smith enjoyed the series' detailed backgrounds.<ref name=":5"/> Te praised each episode's color palette and the choreography's combination of martial arts and magic.<ref name=":11"/> Hartel criticized the animation, although he found it an improvement over previous Nickelodeon shows.<ref name=":0"/> Mitchell called the animation fluid.<ref name=":4"/> Te agreed, noting its manga influence.<ref name=":11"/> According to Brittany Lovely, non-bender characters in battle are "overshadowed" by their bender counterparts.<ref name=":2"/> Joe Corey called the animation's action and environments a "great achievement",<ref name=":3"/> and Keyes praised the series' fight choreography.<ref name=":6"/> According to Hamilton, the action sequences in the series were amazing while being child-appropriate and exciting.<ref name=kirk/>

=== Legacy ===
''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' became a [[Cult following|cult classic]] and had a large impact in the 2010s on how networks viewed animated programs; subsequent children's shows would often blur the lines between youth and adult programming, featuring more adult themes.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/merrillbarr/2013/11/04/three-shows-that-changed-the-way-networks-think-about-viewership/#1bd89fb163cd |title=Three Shows That Changed The Way Networks Think About Viewership |date=November 4, 2013 |magazine=Forbes |access-date=August 17, 2019 |archive-date=September 11, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190911115643/https://www.forbes.com/sites/merrillbarr/2013/11/04/three-shows-that-changed-the-way-networks-think-about-viewership/#1bd89fb163cd |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kirkl |first=Justin |date=May 25, 2020 |title=I Never Gave 'Avatar: The Last Airbender' a Chance. Now I Know What I Was Missing. |url=https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a32597016/avatar-the-last-airbender-netflix/ |access-date=July 27, 2020 |website=Esquire |archive-date=June 19, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200619093719/https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a32597016/avatar-the-last-airbender-netflix/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

Multiple media publications have hailed ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' as one of the greatest animated television series of all time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Quarantine Stream: 'Avatar: The Last Airbender' is an Animated Fantasy Epic That Understands the Devastation of War |url=https://www.slashfilm.com/the-quarantine-stream-avatar-the-last-airbender/ |date=May 17, 2020 |work=Slash Film The series experienced a resurgence in popularity following its addition to [[Netflix]] on May 15, 2020; it reached the number-one position on the platform's top series in the U.S. four days after release, and was the most-popular film or show for the week of May 14–21.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Adalian |first1=Josef |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender Is Netflix's Surprise Summer Hit |url=https://www.vulture.com/2020/06/avatar-last-airbender-netflix-summer-hit.html |work=[[Vulture.com|Vulture]] |publisher=[[Vox Media]] |access-date=January 10, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200620054055/https://www.vulture.com/2020/06/avatar-last-airbender-netflix-summer-hit.html |archive-date=June 20, 2020 |date=June 18, 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> The series maintained a spot within Netflix's top ten series for a record-setting 60 days, the most of any show since the company debuted its list of top series in February 2020.<ref name="Newsweek">{{cite web |last1=Spencer |first1=Samuel |title='Avatar The Last Airbender' Just Broke A Major Netflix Record |url=https://www.newsweek.com/avatar-last-airbender-show-netflix-chart-top-10-record-1519004 |work=[[Newsweek]] |access-date=January 10, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200730084842/https://www.newsweek.com/avatar-last-airbender-show-netflix-chart-top-10-record-1519004 |archive-date=July 30, 2020 |date=July 20, 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> The series would become the most-streamed children's series on the platform for the year.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 9, 2021 |title="Avatar: The Last Airbender" Topped US List of Animated Kids Shows on Netflix in 2020, The NPD Group Says |url=https://www.npd.com/wps/portal/npd/us/news/press-releases/2021/avatar-the-last-airbender-topped-us-list-of-animated-kids-shows-on-netflix--in-2020-the-npd-group-says/ |access-date=February 17, 2021 |website=[[The NPD Group]] |archive-date=February 12, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210212213327/https://www.npd.com/wps/portal/npd/us/news/press-releases/2021/avatar-the-last-airbender-topped-us-list-of-animated-kids-shows-on-netflix--in-2020-the-npd-group-says/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Both fans and co-creators DiMartino and Konietzko attributed ''Avatar: The Last Airbender''{{'}}s renewed popularity to its relevance to contemporary events, including the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and [[2020–2021 United States racial unrest|racial unrest in the U.S.]], with DiMartino remarking: "The major issues in the stories{{emdash}}genocide, totalitarianism, systemic injustice, abuse{{emdash}}sadly, these have been pervasive issues throughout history and continue to be. The show is a reflection of our world. But now, we happen to be living through a time in which all these problems have been exacerbated."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sonde |first1=Kari |title=How 'Avatar: The Last Airbender' became one of the summer's most popular shows — 15 years after its debut |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/entertainment/how-avatar-the-last-airbender-became-one-of-the-summers-most-popular-shows--15-years-after-its-debut/2020/08/06/e368e740-d803-11ea-aff6-220dd3a14741_story.html |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=January 10, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809094944/https://www.washingtonpost.com/entertainment/how-avatar-the-last-airbender-became-one-of-the-summers-most-popular-shows--15-years-after-its-debut/2020/08/06/e368e740-d803-11ea-aff6-220dd3a14741_story.html |archive-date=August 9, 2020 |date=August 7, 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Franchise ==
{{main|Avatar: The Last Airbender (franchise)}}

=== Adaptations ===

==== ''The Last Airbender'' (2010) ====
{{Main|The Last Airbender (film){{!}}''The Last Airbender'' (film)}}

The series' first season was adapted as the 2010 live-action film ''[[The Last Airbender (film)|The Last Airbender]]'', which was written and directed by [[M. Night Shyamalan]] and stars [[Noah Ringer]] as Aang, [[Nicola Peltz]] as Katara, [[Jackson Rathbone]] as Sokka, [[Dev Patel]] as Zuko, and [[Shaun Toub]] as Iroh.<ref name="cast" /> Although the film originally shared the title of the television series, the title ''The Last Airbender'' was used because producers feared it would be confused with [[James Cameron]]'s film ''[[Avatar (2009 film)|Avatar]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stephenson |first=Hunter |date=April 15, 2008 |title=M. Night Shyamalan's The Last Airbender Gets Release Date, Director Update, "Avatar" Dropped From Title |url=http://www.slashfilm.com/2008/04/15/m-night-shyamalans-the-last-airbender-gets-release-date-avatar-dropped-from-title/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170901202851/http://www.slashfilm.com/m-night-shyamalans-the-last-airbender-gets-release-date-avatar-dropped-from-title/ |archive-date=September 1, 2017 |publisher=/Film}}</ref> It was intended as the first of a trilogy of films, each of which would be based upon one of the three television seasons. The film was universally panned for its writing, acting, [[Whitewashing in film|whitewashed]] cast, and Shyamalan's direction; it has a 5% approval rating on [[Rotten Tomatoes]] and earned five [[Razzies]] at the [[31st Golden Raspberry Awards]], including [[Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Picture|Worst Picture]];<ref name="cast">{{Cite web |last=Mahajan |first=Mradula |date=September 30, 2015 |title='Avatar: The Last Airbender' Sequel Update: Trilogy In Making; M. Night Shyamalan To Not Repeat Mistakes of Failed Adaptation! |url=http://www.movienewsguide.com/avatar-the-last-airbender-sequel-update-trilogy-m-night-shyamalan-not-repeat-mistakes/100635 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151005002952/https://www.movienewsguide.com/avatar-the-last-airbender-sequel-update-trilogy-m-night-shyamalan-not-repeat-mistakes/100635 |archive-date=October 5, 2015 |access-date=December 11, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Last Airbender |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/last_airbender/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170830134552/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/last_airbender |archive-date=August 30, 2017 |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |date=February 26, 2011 |title=Razzie Awards: 'The Last Airbender' earns Worst Picture, Director, and 'Eye-Gouging Misuse of 3-D' |url=http://ew.com/article/2011/02/26/razzie-awards-last-airbender-sex-and-the-city-2/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170302165138/http://ew.com/article/2011/02/26/razzie-awards-last-airbender-sex-and-the-city-2/ |archive-date=March 2, 2017 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |title=25 Questions You May Have About The Last Airbender |url=https://www.vanityfair.com/online/oscars/2010/07/25-questions-you-may-have-about-the-last-airbender |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210514191350/https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2010/07/25-questions-you-may-have-about-the-last-airbender |archive-date=May 14, 2021 |access-date=December |website=Hi! Magazine}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Onda |first=David |title=The Last Airbender |url=http://xfinity.comcast.net/slideshow/entertainment-franchiseflops/10/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224104351/http://xfinity.comcast.net/slideshow/entertainment-franchiseflops/10/ |archive-date=December 24, 2013 |access-date=December 22, 2013 |work=Comcast}}</ref>

==== ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' (2024–present) ====
{{Main|Avatar: The Last Airbender (2024 TV series){{!}}''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' (2024 TV series)}}

[[Netflix]] announced in September 2018 that a "reimagined" live-action adaptation of ''Avatar: The Last Airbender'' was to start production in 2019. The series' original creators, DiMartino and Konietzko, were to be the executive producers and [[showrunner]]s.<ref name="Polygon September 2018" /> On August 12, 2020, DiMartino and Konietzko both revealed on their social media that they had departed the show due to creative differences.<ref>{{cite web |last1=DiMartino |first1=Michael |title=An open letter to Avatar: The Last Airbender Fans 2020 |publisher=[[Instagram]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=August 12, 2020 |title=Avatar: The Last Airbender creators quit Netflix live-action adaptation over creative differences |url=https://www.theverge.com/2020/8/12/21365329/avatar-last-airbender-netflix-live-action-michael-dante-dimartino-bryan-konietzko-departure |url-status=live
